author: s6-merge
body:
title: Combine conflicts in this archive are a choice between alternatives, and the score order makes that choice blind
ledger_rows: L5, L6 (and L8 through X2-DT)
concept: A line-based 3-way merge cannot combine two edits that rewrite the same lines. Git also conflicts on edits that are merely adjacent, and on an edit that extends another's hunk (my own git 2.43 test). Structured merge does not rescue this: FSTMerge keeps method bodies "as plain text" and merges them line by line [Apel]. So a conflict between two keeps is a choice. That makes the combine a selection problem: pick the conflict-free subset with the largest gain, which is a maximum-weight independent set on the conflict graph. The order in which keeps are merged is a policy, and phase-ordering theory names its failure mode: one transformation can "irrevocably prevent another ... from triggering" [Tate]. Greedy order decides what survives. When merges are textually clean, gains add nearly linearly, so the loss sits in the choice, not in interaction between merged changes.
source: S. Apel, J. Liebig, B. Brandl, C. Lengauer, C. Kästner, "Semistructured Merge: Rethinking Merge in Revision Control Systems", ESEC/FSE 2011, https://www.se.cs.uni-saarland.de/publications/docs/FSE2011.pdf (full text read). R. Tate, M. Stepp, Z. Tatlock, S. Lerner, "Equality Saturation: A New Approach to Optimization", POPL 2009 / LMCS 2011, https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.1802 (full text read).
worked_example: All numbers are my zero-credit computations on w2-sprint/zero-credit/pairs.csv, q1_left_out.csv and w2-sprint/live/ (scripts in r3/work/s6-merge/).
(1) Of 365 within-run keep pairs, 72 conflict. Every conflicting pair changes overlapping lines inside a function both keeps edit. 36 delete exactly overlapping sets of lines, and none has added-line similarity of 0.9 or more, so these are rival rewrites of the same lines, not extensions of each other.
(2) The default order is hypothesis score (SITE_STACKS=off, used by every archived arm). Of 57 conflict skips, the left-out keep had the higher standalone gain in 30 and not in 27 (median difference +0.11 percentage points): a coin flip.
(3) L6's 12 runs split three ways. In 7, the run's best keep was left out by a conflict (markdown 10.1 delivered against 21.8, and 9.9 against 20.7). In 4, the best keep was applied and the shortfall is 0 to 1.1 percentage points. 1 is the failed mistune combine.
(4) In 54 held combines with 2 or more applied keeps, delivered gain divided by the sum of the applied keeps' standalone gains has a median of 0.91 (IQR 0.82 to 1.00).
prediction: A dry, git-only replay of the 7 L6 runs that lost their best keep, with keeps ordered by mean gain (the conflict-subset logic of plan_delivery with by_gain), applies the best keep in all 7 runs. The summed standalone gain of the applied set rises above the score-ordered set's in at least 6 of the 7. Re-measuring those tips (ABAB only, no API) gives a delivered gain above the archived one in at least 5 of the 7.
limits: Standalone gains are noisy (floors of 2 to 4 %) and selected as maxima, so some "weaker side" verdicts are noise, and choosing by gain inherits a winner's curse. The 0.91 additivity is measured only for textually clean combines of 2 to 5 keeps. It says nothing about 9 to 15 keeps, or about semantic conflicts, which a textual merge cannot see. GEVO found interacting edits to be a key source of speed-up in one of its three programs [errata, source 19]; that is a counter-case to near-additivity. The X2-DT plan refuses SITE_STACKS under stacking, so a stacked round would fix the score-order choice in place. IntelliMerge's published figures are unverified (errata, source 5), so I make no claim that refactoring-aware merge would help.

author: s1-perf-eng
body:
title: The engine's gain is time saved, and time saved on separate code adds up, so a combine below its best part means the best part was dropped
ledger_rows: L6 (main); L5, L8 (same mechanism)
concept: Amdahl's accounting says a change can save only the time spent in the code it touches. Time saved on separate pieces of code therefore adds up. The engine's gain is time saved divided by base time (`anticheat.relative_gain`). So two keeps that change different code should combine to about the sum of their gains, never below the larger one. Two keeps that edit the same lines (a textual conflict) both act on the same slice of time, and only one can be applied. The sensible pick is the one with the larger measured gain. A combine that delivers less than its best single keep therefore has one of three causes:
(a) the best keep was left out;
(b) the parts get in each other's way;
(c) measurement noise, including the fact that the best of several noisy first-look gains is biased upward.
(a) is a combine-ordering loss. (b) and (c) are not.
source: Amdahl, G. M., "Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities", AFIPS SJCC 1967, pp. 483–485, DOI 10.1145/1465482.1465560 (full text read: the IEEE SSCS reprint). Gustafson, J. L., "Reevaluating Amdahl's Law", CACM 31(5), 1988, pp. 532–533, DOI 10.1145/42411.42415 (full text read; it states the formula speedup = 1/(s + p/N), which the Amdahl reprint, by its editors' note, does not contain).
worked_example: I recounted on `w2-sprint/live/`. In 12 of the 65 runs with keeps, the delivered gain is below the run's best first-look keep. In those 12, the median delivered gain is +10.1 against a median best keep of +13.4. The ledger's "+17.4 vs +11.3" does not match this, so please check it.
- The best keep was left out by a textual conflict with a lower-gain keep that was applied, in 6 runs. Five are listed in `zero-credit/q1_left_out.csv`; the sixth is in its run's `skipped` field. The shortfalls in points: X2-0 markdown 316a634f 11.7; X2-D markdown af0d2b9a 10.8; X2-0 markdown 8de73b17 5.4; X2-0 sqlparse 8d4c990c 2.3; X2-0 markdown cdccc54d 1.5; X2-P sqlparse aa4143a6 0.2.
- The combine failed in 1 run (X2-D mistune, 4.0 points; that loss is L7).
- In the other 5, the best keep is not recorded as left out. Their shortfalls are 0.1 to 1.5 points, about the size of re-measuring noise.
- Every shortfall of 5 points or more is a dropped best keep.
- Why the best keep can lose. X2-0 runs no dry merge (`o62/README.md`), and without one `combine_kept` applies keeps in hypothesis-score order (`combine_node.py`, sort by −score), not in order of measured gain. The by-gain max-sum plan (`plan_delivery`, S2) already exists in the code.
prediction: This needs no API spend. In the 6 conflict runs, replay the archived diffs in measured-gain order (S2's plan), with the best keep replacing the keep that blocked it, and re-measure the tip with ABAB. I predict: in at least 4 of the 6, the delivered gain rises by more than that run's floor; the two markdown runs with shortfalls of 10 points or more (316a634f, af0d2b9a) each recover at least +5 points. The idea is wrong for L6 if fewer than 3 of the 6 improve.
limits:
- Gains are not strictly additive. Two changes can get in each other's way: one can invalidate what the other relies on, or both can compete for the same cache. A swapped-in best keep may also conflict with other keeps that were applied.
- First-look gains are noisy, and the maximum of several is biased upward. That is fp-measure's ground, and it probably explains the 5 small shortfalls.
- Amdahl prices the time at the place a change touches. It does not say whether the profiled shares of time are right.
- A conflict can join two different mechanisms on the same code. When both could be merged, the best answer may be a hand-merged union rather than a choice of one.

author: fp-compose
body:
title: Disjoint keeps add their saved fractions, so combine loss is a selection problem, not an arithmetic one
ledger_rows: L5, L6 (also bears on L8)
concept: The engine scores a gain as time saved divided by base time (`anticheat.relative_gain`). If a change speeds up a fraction f of the run by a factor S, it saves f(1 − 1/S) of base time (Amdahl). So two changes that act on disjoint time, each measured against the same base, compose by adding their saved fractions: G = Σgᵢ. The speed-ups do not multiply. Only overlapping changes, which spend the same time, fall below the sum. Interaction is the measurable departure from additivity, and it is usually small. So when a combine delivers less than its parts promise, look first at which parts were chosen and whether they overlap, not at the arithmetic. Choosing among conflicting keeps is a max-weight conflict-free subset problem. A greedy order by any other key (score, round) can lose to it. The subset is chosen on noisy single looks, so its total is optimistic (the optimizer's curse).
source:
- Hill, M. D., & Marty, M. R. (2008). Amdahl's Law in the Multicore Era. IEEE Computer 41(7), 33–38. https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2008.209 (full text read). The "Amdahl's Law" sidebar gives Speedup(f, S) = 1/((1 − f) + f/S) and notes that Amdahl's 1967 paper argued "without presenting an equation".
- Siegmund, N. et al. (2012). Predicting Performance via Automated Feature-Interaction Detection. ICSE 2012, 167–177. https://www.se.cs.uni-saarland.de/publications/docs/ICSE2012.pdf (full text read). The paper reports 95 % average prediction accuracy over six case studies when interactions are modelled, "a 15 percent improvement over an approach that takes no interactions into account".
- The saved-time additive form is my derivation from the fraction form, not a quotation.
worked_example: One run where the sum holds: X2-0 43080309535 tomli applied three keeps of +12.0, +5.4 and +6.8. The sum predicts +24.2; the combine delivered +24.8 (`w2-sprint/live/` rows).
Across 61 held combines, delivered gain over the sum of the applied keeps' standalone gains has: a median of 0.94, IQR 0.82–1.01, range 0.48–1.24; an aggregate of 0.88, that is 1,123 of 1,277 points. So additivity is off by about 6–12 %, the same order as Siegmund's interaction error.
The loss is in selection:
- Better subsets existed. The exact max-sum conflict-free subset of each run's keeps totals 1,464 standalone points against the 1,277 applied. That is +3.06 per row, with 21 of 61 rows above 1 pp. At 0.88 it is worth about 2.7 delivered pp per run. Conflicts come from a hunk-range proxy that agrees with zero-credit's `git merge-file` replay on 363 of 365 pairs.
- Score order can bury the best keep. In 7 of the 12 L6 rows, the best keep was blocked by a conflict with a higher-scored keep, losing 33.4 pp in total.
- Gain order already exists in code. `plan_delivery(by_gain=True)`, under `SITE_STACKS="on"` in `orchestrator/combine_node.py`, offers this subset first. The archived arms ran with it off.
Scripts: `r3/work/fp-compose/l5all.py`, `l6b.py`.
prediction: Re-measure, with zero API spend, the tips of the max-sum subsets in the 21 rows where they beat the applied set. Their delivered gain should be about 0.88 × the subset's standalone sum, within the observed IQR (0.82–1.01 of that sum), and should beat the archived delivered gain by about 6 pp per row on average (≈ 0.88 × 136 points over 21 rows, given the 187-point aggregate excess). Two outcomes would refute the lesson as it applies here: a median ratio below 0.75 on those tips (the newly chosen keeps interact or overlap more than the applied ones); a mean uplift under 2 pp per row.
limits:
- Additivity needs the keeps to act on disjoint time and to be measured against the same base. For overlapping changes (O: a different change on the same hunks, 36 left-out keeps carrying 336 standalone points), the sum is only an upper bound. Their true marginal lies anywhere from 0 to the smaller gain, which only stacking or a re-apply-and-measure can settle.
- True repeats (21 of 57 conflicts) add about 0.
- The subset is picked on single noisy looks, so its total overstates (Smith & Winkler 2006; I have only the abstract and the authors' correction, so this part is unverified).
- Conflicts are textual. A pair can merge cleanly and still interact semantically, and the 0.48 low of the ratio shows this happens.
- One row (X2-D 43159154661 mistune, 1 of 7 keeps delivered) is my inference of a failed greedy combine with no `fallback_trial_id` to confirm it.
- Under stacked rounds (X2-DT), gains are measured against a moving tip, so they must be rescaled by (1 − G) before they are added.

author: z1-analogy
body:
title: A second look should be pooled with the first, not required to pass alone (two-stage screens, genetics)
ledger_rows: L4 (primary); L3 (the part that reaches confirmation)
concept: In a two-stage screen, stage 1 tests everything and stage 2 retests only the promising part. Requiring stage 2 to be significant on its own ("replication-based analysis") throws away stage 1's evidence. Skol et al. show that a joint test over both stages, with a stricter threshold that keeps the same false-positive rate, has more power to detect true effects. The joint test decides whether a change is kept. The size of the effect is still estimated from data that did not select it, because the look that selected a hit overstates it (the winner's curse, Zöllner and Pritchard). The structure carries over unchanged: the engine's first look is stage 1, and its confirmation look is stage 2.
source: Skol, Scott, Abecasis and Boehnke, "Joint analysis is more efficient than replication-based analysis for two-stage genome-wide association studies", Nature Genetics 38(2):209-213, 2006, doi:10.1038/ng1706. I could not read Skol's own text (closed). Its core result is confirmed from the full text of an open paper that restates it: Sha, Zhang and Zhang, "Joint Analysis for Genome-Wide Association Studies in Family-Based Designs", PLoS ONE, 2011, PMC3142116. Skol's qualifiers ("almost always", "robust when effect sizes differ") are unverified (my errata). For the winner's curse: Zöllner and Pritchard, Am. J. Hum. Genet. 80(4):605-615, 2007, doi:10.1086/512821, full text read.
worked_example: Today's rule. `orchestrator/confirm.py:confirm_one` re-tests a would-be keep with `retest_one`. If that second look alone does not hold, the verdict becomes `inconclusive` and the first look's evidence is discarded. `reported_gain` averages the two looks, but only for the report.
The loss. `floors/README.md` s3 counts 284 keeps and 49 inconclusives that cleared their own floor on the first look. The README infers these 49 are failed second looks. So 49 / 333 = 14.7 % of first-look passes fail confirmation (my computation).
The transfer. I modelled each look as z ~ N(δ, 1), with a first-look threshold of 2, and kept today's conjunction false-positive rate of 2.28 % squared, which is 5.2e-4. The matched joint rule (first look > 2, then mean z > 3.19) gives this power (my computation, `r3/work/z1-analogy/twostage.py`): δ 2.0: conjunction 0.250, joint 0.294; δ 2.5: 0.478, 0.547; δ 3.0: 0.708, 0.776. That is about +7 points of power at the same false-positive rate. The reported gain stays the second look, or the delivery re-test.
prediction: If the 49 lost confirmations are mostly true effects lost to noise, which is the regime where a joint test helps, then their first-look gain / own-floor ratio is not concentrated at the floor. I predict that the median of that ratio over the 49 is at least 1.3. If it is below 1.15, they are mainly marginal first looks (selection and winner's curse), and pooling would admit mostly noise. This can be tested from the archived rows (the first-look gain and floor columns that `floors/README.md` used, `q3_list.csv` and its source rows).
limits:
- Independence. The model assumes the two looks are independent. `floors/README.md` s4 shows high floors cluster by run (90 of 175 in the noisiest 10 runs, p < 0.0005) and fall with time since the start. Correlated looks shrink the power gain and miscalibrate the joint threshold. It must be set for the engine's own floor statistic, not a z-test.
- Missing data. The second look's gain is not archived for the failed confirmations. Without it, the 49 cannot be re-scored offline yet.
- The effect is modest. It does nothing for L3 trials that never reach confirmation.
- What it changes. It changes the decision rule in `confirm.py`, not `judges.py`, so it is the owner's call.

author: s4-algorithms
body:
title: How much a change removing a super-linear term gains depends on input size; a doubling probe shows that size dependence without any API call
ledger_rows: L3, L8, L1
concept: When a change removes a super-linear term (for example a slice copy inside a loop, a tuple grown with `+=`, or a cache cleared on every call), its gain grows with the input size n. A fixed benchmark measures that gain at one n only. Sedgewick's doubling experiment makes the dependence visible: run the hot path at N, 2N and 4N and read the ratio T(2N)/T(N). Under the tilde model g(N) ~ a·f(N), with f(N) = N^b log^c N, the ratio approaches 2^b. That reading of the ratio is my own derivation from the model on the booksite, not a sentence on the page (errata [3]). The probe compares two timings of the same code version at different sizes, so it can tell a small gain from a constant-factor fix apart from a small gain where the benchmark's n hides a quadratic term. Use it as triage, to ground and rank ideas, never as a judge.
source: R. Sedgewick, K. Wayne, *Algorithms*, 4th ed., Addison-Wesley 2011, ISBN 978-0-321-57351-3. Full text read: booksite §1.4, https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/14analysis/ (tilde notation, the DoublingRatio program). The book itself was not accessed, so it is an open substitute.
worked_example: These are my own measurements from the notes, §1 table: CPython 3.13.16 on the round VM, min of 3, script `r3/work/s4-algorithms/bench/doubling.py`. They are not archive numbers. A regex tokeniser that calls `match(s[pos:])` takes 1.98 ms at 10k characters, with doubling ratios of 2.66 and then 3.62. The same tokeniser calling `match(s, pos)` takes 1.43 ms, with ratios of 2.02 and 1.97. Multiplying through gives times of 1.98, 5.27 and 19.07 ms against 1.43, 2.89 and 5.69 ms at 10k, 20k and 40k characters. So one and the same diff is worth +38 %, +82 % and +235 %. The size of the benchmark sets the measured gain. The archive has gains in the same small band. L3 has 47 inconclusive trials whose gain sat above the baseline floor but below their own floor, with a median of 3.8 % and 10 of them at 5 % or more (`w2-sprint/floors/README.md` s3, via the ledger). L8's unique keeps per run fall from 1.75 to 0.83 to 0.42 (X2-D, `zero-credit/README.md` s2). In both cases the data cannot say which small gains come from n and which from constant factors. A doubling ratio can. Decoy and trap pair, from the same table: `self.out += s` has ratios of 3.92 and 4.03, while a local `+=` has 1.98 and 2.00 and is not slow.
prediction: Re-run the hot call chain of each of L3's 47 inconclusive diffs on the benchmark input copied to 2x and 4x size. At least 5 of the 47 (≥ 10 %) will show T(2n)/T(n) ≥ 2.6 on the baseline and ≤ 2.2 with the diff applied. Those diffs will fall into the mechanism classes in §3 of my notes (membership test on a list, FIFO built on a list, slice copy, recompute instead of maintain, rescan with `re.search`). The rest will show the same ratio, within ±0.2, on both sides.
limits: The probe changes the input, so it is never a judge and never a reason to change a benchmark (benchmarks are FIXED). A gain that appears only at 2n does not count toward the engine's verdict. Its value is in ranking ideas and grounding them (L1's 31 `ungrounded`), and in telling whether L8's decay is a property of the code or of the input size. Ratios read wrongly in four situations. At small n, timer noise and fixed start-up cost dominate. Cache effects, memory allocation and GC can push a ratio above 2 with no algorithmic cause. Amortised resizing produces spikes on the call that resizes (MIT 6.046 L5). Scaled copies of the input can scale the wrong dimension; for example, doubling the document is not the same as doubling the number of reference definitions in one block. The 2^b reading is my derivation, and it fails when the log^c term is large.

author: z3-contrarian
body:
title: An inconclusive trial is mostly a real gain too small to see. Choose them by call count, not by timing, and test them as a bundle
ledger_rows: L3, L4 (also L1, which counts ideas but not their gain)
concept: The engine judges each idea alone, with 5 timed runs a side, and drops anything below that trial's own noise floor. But the inconclusive pile is mostly small real gains, not nulls. Mature projects that grew by many sub-1 % changes did not see those changes with wall-clock timing. SQLite counted instructions with cachegrind; Meta's FBDetect measured at subroutine level. Each change was screened by a measurement that does not move between runs, and kept if it added up. This engine already has such a measurement: `op_count`, the deterministic number of calls in each trial row. The proposed mechanism: use the call count only to choose which inconclusives go into a bundle, never the noisy gain, which would pick the lucky ones. Then let the frozen judges time the bundle once.
source: SQLite, "Measuring and Reducing CPU Usage in SQLite", https://www.sqlite.org/cpu.html, and D. R. Hipp, "[sqlite] 50% faster than 3.7.17", sqlite-users, 19 Sep 2014, https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@sqlite.org/msg86235.html (full text read for both, errata [12]). Hipp: each micro-optimisation might be worth "as little as 0.05%" and is "unmeasurable on a real-world system". cpu.html: wall-clock run times are "scarcely repeatable beyond one significant digit", while cachegrind is repeatable to "7 or more significant digits". Second source: Yoon et al. (Meta), "FBDetect", SOSP 2024, https://tangchq74.github.io/FBDetect-SOSP24.pdf (full text read, errata [14]). Its §1 example: a 0.005 % regression in a service becomes a 5 % change when measured in the one subroutine, using 0.1 % of CPU, that caused it.
worked_example: Source: the trial rows in `w2-sprint/live/` (63 runs, 974 trials, X2-SV left out), each with `gain_pct`, `verdict` and `op_count.change`; my scripts `a.py`, `c.py` and `d.py` in r3/work/z3-contrarian/.
- **The inconclusives lean positive.** 467 of 641 are above zero (73 %), mean +1.10 %, sign test z = 11.6.
- **The measurement is not what makes them positive.** The 58 inconclusives whose call count did not change at all average +0.12 %.
- **The gain rises with the call cut:**

  | Call-count change | Inconclusives | Mean gain | Share positive |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | cut 10 % or more | 27 | +3.78 % | 100 % |
  | cut 1 to 10 % | 314 | +1.54 % | 83 % |
  | within 1 % | 265 | +0.36 % | 59 % |

  Spearman between call change and gain is -0.37 over all inconclusives, and negative in every library: markdown -0.46, mistune -0.40, sqlparse -0.31, tomli -0.24.
- **What a bundle could hold.** Per run, choosing only by a call cut of 1 % or more gives a median of 5 inconclusives, summing to +6.7 points (IQR 4.2 to 10.2). Leaving out those whose target function an applied keep already edits, it is still +4.5 points (IQR 1.7 to 8.1). The median delivered gain is +17.4.
- **The engine's own pairs already work.** Near-miss pairs (X2-D compounds) were kept 12 of 16 times, against 84 of 378 for single X2-D trials.
prediction: On the next live run's rows, inconclusive trials whose call count fell by 1 % or more will be positive in at least 75 % of cases, with a mean gain of at least +1.2 %. Those with exactly no change in calls will average within ±0.5 % of zero. In the archive today: 77 to 90 % positive per library, mean +1.60 to +1.86 %, and +0.12 % for no change. When the inconclusive-diff archive arrives (O63 item 5), a bundle chosen only by call count and applied on the held tip will clear the frozen judges' floor in at least half of the runs. If it clears in fewer, the mechanism is dead.
limits:
- **Call count is not time.** Work done inside a regex or a C-level string method can change time with no change in calls; the within-1 % group still averages +0.36 %. Inlining a call lowers the count with almost no saving. The count is a screen and a way to choose, never the judge; the frozen judges decide every keep.
- **Additivity is measured on keeps only.** Delivered gain over the sum of the applied keeps' own gains has a median of 0.91. Sub-floor diffs may overlap more than that, or conflict as text. And only keeps' diffs are archived today, so the bundle test must wait for the inconclusive-diff archive.
- **What would make it wrong.** If the positive lean comes from a shared bias on the B side that the no-change group does not show, for example warm-up or ordering in the ABBA design, the effect would be an artefact. This holds especially if L4's failed second looks turn out to be real nulls.
- **Where it does not carry over.** SQLite and FBDetect are C and C++. Whether CPython's call count is as good a screen as an instruction count is contested.

author: s7-cpython
body:
title: cProfile charges for every call it sees, so profile shares overrate call removal and underrate hoisting work out of call-dense loops
ledger_rows: L1, L3, L10
concept: cProfile is a deterministic profiler. It pays a cost on every call and return event, and since 3.12 it does so through sys.monitoring. Turning on the CALL event rewrites every call site as `INSTRUMENTED_CALL`, which, per PEP 669, "will interfere with specialization". So the overhead is not uniform: it grows with how many events a region fires. Code dense in calls, including calls to C builtins, is inflated; a loop that makes no calls is not. A share read off cProfile is therefore biased toward ideas that remove calls, and against ideas that remove work from a loop that stays call-dense. The engine uses cProfile shares three ways: it ranks hotspots by self time, it shows them to the lanes, and it computes each idea's Amdahl ceiling from cProfile cumulative time (`idea_context.amdahl_ceiling`). All three inherit the bias.
source: Shannon, M., "PEP 669: Low Impact Monitoring for CPython", 2021, https://peps.python.org/pep-0669/ (full text read). CPython `Modules/_lsprof.c`: the 3.11 branch uses `PyEval_SetProfile`, 3.12 registers `PY_MONITORING_EVENT`s (full text read). Berger, Stern, Altmayer Pizzorno, "Triangulating Python Performance Issues with Scalene", OSDI 2023, Table 3: cProfile median slowdown 1.73x, range 1.35x to 2.63x, https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi23-berger.pdf (full text read).
worked_example: Fixtures, from my library notes (`r3/work/s7-cpython/exp/plants.py`, one VM, best of 7 plain and best of 5 profiled, not ABBA):
- Inlining a helper called on every element gained 24-27% for real, but 70-83% when timed under cProfile.
- Hoisting a table that a caller rebuilt on every call gained 72-76% for real, but 28-48% under cProfile.
- Within one interpreter, cProfile's slowdown ranged from 1.02x (a loop with no calls) to 8.1x (one `re.match` per token).

Archive (my computation, today, over `w2-sprint/live/ideas-x2-*.jsonl`, X2-SV excluded): 972 trials record `op_count`.
- The 42 trials that cut Python calls by 20% or more gained a median of 11.9%. The median ratio of gain to call cut is 0.46.
- The 648 trials that changed calls by less than 5% gained a median of 1.0%.

So a cut in measured calls buys only about half its size in time, while cProfile prices calls at several times their real cost.
prediction: Regress `gain_pct` on the call cut (`-op_count.change`) over the 302 archive trials that cut calls by 5% or more. The slope will fall between 0.3 and 0.6, well below 1. The slope's confidence interval will exclude 1. I have not run this; the 0.46 above comes from the n = 42 subset only.
limits:
- `op_count` counts calls; it is not a time. Trials that cut calls usually change other things too, so the slope is a correlation, not a price per call.
- My fixtures are tiny, from one noisy VM, and not ABBA.
- On 3.11 the hook is `setprofile`, so the specialisation cost does not apply.
- The claim covers single-threaded, CPU-bound Python only.
- A sampling profiler (py-spy, Austin, Tachyon) would remove most of this bias. If its shares agree with cProfile's on the archived workloads, within its sampling error (±0.5 points at 100,000 samples), the bias is too small to matter here and the claim is wrong for this engine.

author: s2-stats
body:
title: The noise sits in the runs, not the timer, so X2-DT's pre-registered read can only see a large effect
ledger_rows: L9 (main), L8, L7
concept: Kalibera and Jones split benchmark variation into levels, such as build, execution and iteration. Each level has its own variance component T²ᵢ and its own cost cᵢ. Repetition must happen at the highest level that varies; repeating a lower level only saves time. The optimal count for a lower level is rᵢ = ⌈√(c₍ᵢ₊₁₎·T²ᵢ / (cᵢ·T²₍ᵢ₊₁₎))⌉. In this engine the levels are "a run" (ideation, editing, combine) and "a look" (one timed re-test of a tip). When nearly all the variance is at the run level, more looks buy no precision. Only more runs, or a sharper statistic, buy precision. With 20 runs against 20, the sign test can only detect a large effect.
source: Kalibera, T., Jones, R., "Rigorous Benchmarking in Reasonable Time", ISMM 2013, doi:10.1145/2464157.2464160, s3 and eq. 3 in s9.3. Full text read (author's manuscript, https://kar.kent.ac.uk/33611/). The rule's code is `services/python_agents/tests/live/ideas_x2_report.py:872-917` (`sign_call`).
worked_example:
- **The two variance components.** X2-D's 20 delivered gains have a per-library sd of 4.25 (tomli), 10.86 (sqlparse), 9.22 (mistune) and 4.83 (markdown) points (`w2-sprint/o61/variance-x2-d-20-not-preregistered.md` s2). On the replay, each re-measured tip moved by at most 1.3 points over 3 looks, an sd of 0.15 to 0.75 (`o62/replay.md` s1). Measurement is therefore about 0.35/61, under 1 % of the run-level variance.
- **Eq. 3.** A look costs about 13 s (replay s2) and a run about 2,400 s (35 to 45 minute dispatches, `floors/README.md` s5B). That gives r = ⌈√(2400/13 × 0.0057)⌉ = 2 looks a run, at most.
- **The pre-registered rule** (`stacked-plan.md` s1). The exact null re-deals each library's 5 + 5 values, so the per-library sign sum is ±5, ±3 or ±1, with counts 21, 45 and 60 out of 252. Its variance is 7.86, against 5 for independent signs.
  - The rule needs **16 of 20** runs above (two-sided 0.0465). 15 of 20 gives 0.108; a naive binomial test would accept 15.
  - My simulation at X2-D's sds (`r3/work/s2-stats/power.py`, `power2.py`) gives 50 % power at about +5.4 points and 80 % at about +8. X2-D's median delivered gain is +18.6.
prediction:
- Add +δ to each of X2-D's 20 archived delivered gains and re-run `sign_call` against the pool on the variance-x2-d-20 page.
- At δ = 0 it reads 14 above, p 0.3837, which reproduces the page.
- From δ = +2.5 to +6.0 it reads 16 above, p 0.1045 to 0.1042, which fails.
- It first passes at δ = +6.5, with 17 above and p 0.0426.
- The script is `r3/work/s2-stats/seminar_check.py`.
limits:
- **A location shift is assumed.** Stacking may change the spread or the tail instead of the centre, for example through path dependence or early stops.
- **The sds are volatile.** They come from 5 runs per library, and an sd from 5 runs has a 90 % interval of 0.42 to 1.54 times the true value.
- **The measurement share is a lower bound.** It comes from a quiet replay, and live in-run looks are noisier: combine floors ran 2.5x to 3.4x the baseline. Even so, the look level stays small against 4 to 11 points.
- **A rank test does not rescue this archive.** A stratified rank-sum test is more powerful in simulation (80 % at about +5.5 points), but on the actual X2-D against pool data it gives p 0.469, worse than the sign test's 0.384.
- **This says nothing about per-trial keeps (L3, L4).** There, measurement noise is the whole story.

author: z2-contradiction
body:
title: A second look is honest only if it was planned in advance and something other than the verdict triggers it
ledger_rows: L3, L4, L7
concept: The contradiction is that N must be large for ambiguous trials and small for the rest. TRIZ resolves it with separation upon condition (repeat only some looks) and separation in time (take the repeat at the quiet end). Statistics adds two binding constraints. First, the looks must be planned in advance. Under Pocock's boundary every look uses the same stricter nominal level for an overall 0.05: 0.0294 a look with 2 looks, 0.0221 with 3, 0.0158 with 5. The number of looks is fixed at the start, and "it is not possible ... to add analyses after the trial has started". Second, the trigger for a look must be blind to the verdict. Monitoring with fixed-horizon tests and stopping on a pass gives "very high false positive probabilities": "Type I error can easily increase fivefold" even at 10,000 samples. So a re-look is legitimate only when a verdict-blind condition triggers it and the number of looks is declared beforehand.
source:
- Pocock, S. J. (1977), "Group sequential methods in the design and analysis of clinical trials", Biometrika 64(2) 191-199, doi:10.1093/biomet/64.2.191. The paper itself is unverified (closed). The boundary values come from its open substitute, Wikipedia "Pocock boundary" (oldid 1308708653, full text read).
- Johari, R., Pekelis, L. and Walsh, D., "Always Valid Inference: Continuous Monitoring of A/B Tests", arXiv:1512.04922v3 (2019), section 1, full text read. This is the companion paper, not KDD '17 (errata [14]).
worked_example:
- **Today's keep rule** (`orchestrator/confirm.py`) already has two fixed looks. A keep or review gets exactly one `retest_one`; `inconclusive` is terminal.
- **The archive** (`w2-sprint/floors/README.md`):
  - s3: 641 inconclusive, 284 keep, 49 reject. 47 inconclusives gained between the baseline floor and their own (median 3.8 % against an own floor of 6.6 %; 10 at 5 % or more). Another 49 cleared their own floor on the first look and then failed the second.
  - s2 and s4: 175 of 972 trials (18.0 %) have a floor above 1.5x the calibrated floor. That share falls from 27 % in minutes 0-5 to 10 % in minutes 30-60, and the noisiest 10 runs hold 90 of the 175.
- **The lesson applied:**
  - A trigger of "own floor > 1.5x the calibrated floor", with one extra look at the run's end, is verdict-blind and declared in advance: 175 trials, about 2.8 a run.
  - Re-looking the 49 because they failed reads the verdict, so it is peeking.
  - In Pocock terms, adding any third look means declaring it first and tightening the per-look level from 0.0294 to the 3-look 0.0221.
prediction: A floor-only trigger reaches the between-floor cases without reading their verdict. Joining `q3_list.csv` with the per-trial floors, I predict that at least 35 of the 47 have an own floor above 1.5x their run's calibrated floor. If fewer than 24 do, the verdict-blind trigger misses most of the target, and C1 loses its case.
limits:
- The engine's judge is "gain > floor", not a p-value, so the Pocock levels are an analogue that shows the direction and size of the tightening, not a correction to apply as is.
- "The run's end is quiet" is a tendency, not a rule. X2-P 43107418692 read 3.37x at about minute 23 after 14 quiet trials (floors s4).
- Run-level false keeps still grow with the number of trials given an extra look.
- My claim that a fresh look after selection is not inflated is my own reasoning, not a sourced result.
- Pocock's paper and the KDD '17 text were not read.

author: s8-expert
body:
title: Experts fix code a profiler never charges; the engine's grounding rule allows only code it does charge
ledger_rows: L10, L1, L5, L8
concept: In real performance work, much of the gain sits outside the functions a profiler ranks highest:
  - in a module-level regex constant;
  - in a data structure built elsewhere;
  - in set-up or a caller;
  - or spread over several files.
  A deterministic profiler charges C-level time, for example `re` matching, to the Python frame that calls it. So a slow regex shows up as a hot dispatcher, never as the constant to fix. SWE-fficiency finds that "over 68% of expert gains occur in functions the LM never edits". The engine has this blind spot by construction: `idea_lanes._ground` drops any non-obvious idea whose quote "lies outside every hot function". The shown hot functions are 8: the top 8 by cumulative time among the 30 top hot spots by self time. An engine that may only edit charged functions converges on fast paths and caches inside those 8, and re-finds them, which produces repeats.
source:
  - Ma et al., "SWE-fficiency: Can Language Models Optimize Real-World Repositories on Real Workloads?", 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06090 (full text read; Section 4, Appendix I, Tables 9-10).
  - Curtsinger and Berger, "Coz: Finding Code that Counts with Causal Profiling", SOSP 2015, https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.03676 (full text read). In dedup the hot line was a hash-bucket search and the fix was three lines in the hash function, +8.95 %. In SQLite the three functions that mattered were at 0.15 % of runtime under perf, and the fix gave +25.60 %.
  - Python 3.11 docs, "The Python Profilers" (full text read).
  - Engine code: optimization/idea_lanes.py, idea_context.py, execution/profiler.py, common/config.py (IDEAS_HOT_FUNCTIONS = 8).
worked_example: I took the 84 real speed commits in the four development libraries' histories (r3/s8/work/classify.tsv) and mapped their changed lines to functions with ast.
  - 85.4 % of the 4,494 changed lines lie outside every function the engine edited in any archived run (52 of 78 commits touch none).
  - On a cProfile of the engine benchmark at each commit's parent (56 commits), applying the engine's 30/8 rule leaves 86.7 % of lines outside the shown functions (42 of 56 commits touch none).
  - Widening the shown set barely helps: top 16, 75.7 % outside (30 commits touch none); top 30, 62.6 % (26); 60/60, 57.5 % (22) (r3/work/s8-expert/seminar-turn1-hotset-widening.txt).
  - So the miss is structural, not a cutoff. Examples:
    - markdown has 8 regex-constant fixes;
    - tomli 7e7658c replaces a set of tuples with a trie, +80 % on the engine's own benchmark (my ABBA, 2 passes).
  - The engine's 284 keeps include 0 data-structure keeps (out of 21 trials).
prediction: Map the changed lines of the engine's 284 kept diffs onto the 8 shown hot functions of each run's base profile. At least 85 % will fall inside them, against 13.3 % for the expert commits. The engine sits at the other end of the same distribution.
limits:
  - Line share is a proxy for gain. Weighted by the five gains confirmed by ABBA (117.8 points), 48 % lies outside the shown functions by line fraction, but only 13 % by whole commit (41 % without 7e7658c), because the largest expert gain had its hot spot in the top 8.
  - 29 of the 84 commits are DoS fixes. Their cost never appears on typical benchmarks, so they inflate the outside share.
  - The hot sets are my reconstruction from my own cProfile runs, not the engine's recorded contexts.
  - Historical function names inflate the "never edited" count.
  - If the prediction fails (the engine already edits outside the shown 8 often), the grounding rule is not the bottleneck.

author: s5-search
body:
title: Failed confirmations (L4) are what the optimizer's curse predicts, before any VM noise is involved

ledger_rows: L4 (primary), L3, L7

concept: The optimizer's curse. Suppose we pick the options whose estimates look best, using estimates that are unbiased but noisy. Then the chosen option's true value is expected to fall below its estimate: "we should expect the value of the chosen alternative to be less than its estimate, even if the value estimates are unbiased". The proposed remedy is Bayesian adjustment of the estimates, "disciplined skepticism". In search terms, an elitist filter keeps lucky draws. Flageat and Cully say the same of MAP-Elites: "standard QD algorithms maintain lucky solutions due to their elitism". Their remedy is to re-evaluate what was kept and decide on the running average. The engine's confirmation step is exactly such a selection: a trial is re-tested only because its first look cleared the floor. So a share of failed second looks is the expected regression toward the mean, even on a machine with no drift at all.

source:
- Smith, J. E. and Winkler, R. L. "The Optimizer's Curse: Skepticism and Postdecision Surprise in Decision Analysis." Management Science 52(3):311-322, 2006. doi:10.1287/mnsc.1050.0451. Full text read (author's copy). The quote is verbatim from the abstract, p. 311, per my errata, which corrected my notes' paraphrase.
- Flageat, M. and Cully, A. "Uncertain Quality-Diversity", 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.00463. Full text read.

worked_example: These numbers come from `w2-sprint/floors/README.md` section 3:
- 284 keeps;
- 49 inconclusives that cleared their own floor on the first look.

That gives 333 first-look passes, of which 49 (14.7 %) failed the second look. My Gaussian model, which is arithmetic and not from a source, runs as follows:
- With 5 runs a side, the sd of a difference of means is σ_d = 0.632 s, where s is the per-run sd.
- The trial floor of 2 sd of one side is then 3.16 σ_d. A null trial passes one look with probability 0.08 %.
- A true gain sitting exactly at the floor fails the second look 50 % of the time; one σ_d above the floor, 16 %.
- 14.7 % therefore corresponds to an average true margin of about 1.05 σ_d above the floor. No VM noise is needed to produce it.

One single case, X2-D 43145496896 on mistune, shows the same pattern (`zero-credit/README.md` s3; `o62/replay.md`):
- First look: d11a38da at +12.51 % against a floor of 7.38.
- Re-test: +8.54 against 9.76, failed.
- Three quiet replays: +10.5 to +11.8.
- The first look sat above all three replays, which is the curse in miniature.

prediction:
- **Test:** in the hypothesis rows under `w2-sprint/live/` (`gain_pct`, `floor_pct`, `verdict`), take the first-look passes, meaning rows with gain_pct > floor_pct and a verdict of keep or inconclusive. Band them by r = gain_pct / floor_pct.
- **Predicted:** the share ending inconclusive is at least 3 times higher for r in (1, 1.25] than for r > 2. The 49 have a median r below 1.5.
- **Kill:** if the failure share is roughly flat across bands (a ratio under 1.5x), selection is not the main cause of L4. VM drift or other judges then dominate.

limits:
- The rows hold one gain per trial. I assume it is the first look, as the floors README's own inference does. If it is the second look, the test does not apply.
- Second-look samples are not archived (`Measurement.samples`), so the model is checked only indirectly.
- The noise is not Gaussian or stationary: there is a heavy tail of slow runs, and floors fall with minutes since the job started (floors README s4). Confirmations run later in the job, so they are quieter, which would push the failure share below the model.
- Some failures may come from the `keep`-only accept rule or other judges, not from the gain. The row does not record the reason.
- This is not a proposal to change any judge. The only lever it implies is outside the judges: how keeps are reported and ranked, for example the mean of both looks, which `confirm.reported_gain` already reports.

author: fp-measure
body:
title: The trial floor prices the spread of single runs, not the uncertainty of the gain, so most failed confirmations are the cost of the measurement itself
ledger_rows: L4 (main), L3, L7
concept: The GUM separates the spread of single observations from the uncertainty of their mean: the mean's standard uncertainty is s/√n (4.2.3, Eq. 5). For a difference of two 5-run means it is s·√(2/5) = 0.632 s. The engine's trial floor is 2·max(sd_A, sd_B) of single runs, which sits at about 3.16 standard errors of the gain it judges. The spread estimate itself is unreliable at n = 5: its relative standard deviation is 36 % (GUM Table E.1). For a process under statistical control, 4.2.4 prefers a pooled sd over a fresh per-measurement s. So the gain has its own noise, about a third of the floor, and selection by a first look biases that look upward. A trial that clears its floor by a small margin will often fail a second look, even when nothing is wrong with the trial, the editor or the runner.
source: JCGM 100:2008, Evaluation of measurement data: Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement, 2008, https://www.bipm.org/documents/20126/2071204/JCGM_100_2008_E.pdf. Full text read: 4.2.3, 4.2.4, 4.2.7, E.4.3 and Table E.1 (library/sources/fp-measure/1-gum.pdf; errata [1]).
worked_example:
- **The rule.** The floor is max(2 sd_A, 2 sd_B, calibrated floor × mean_A) over 5 runs a side (`anticheat.py:207-217`; `floors/README.md` s0).
- **Prediction from the atoms.** If both sides had independent noise with sd = floor/2, the gain's sd per look would be 0.316 × floor.
- **Data.** Of 972 trials (`floors/trials.csv`), 333 cleared their own floor on the first look: 284 kept and 49 inconclusive. Failure rate by first-look gain/floor, my computation (`r3/work/fp-measure/a1.py`, `fit2.py`):

  | Gain/floor | Failed | Rate |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 1-1.25 | 25 of 54 | 46 % |
  | 1.25-1.5 | 13 of 44 | 30 % |
  | 1.5-2 | 10 of 67 | 15 % |
  | 2-3 | 1 of 75 | 1 % |
  | 3+ | 0 of 93 | 0 % |

- **Fit.** I fitted the per-look gain sd as k × floor in an empirical-Bayes model, with the prior estimated from all trial gains (`fit.py`). The best fits are k = 0.35-0.40 for trials at their run's calibrated floor and about 0.3 for trials whose floor is above 1.2x it. Both are close to the 0.316 the atoms predict.
- **Result.** At k = 0.4 the model expects about 53 failed confirmations in total (49 observed), and 26 / 14 / 12 / 1.5 / 0 by bin against 25 / 13 / 10 / 1 / 0 observed. 38 of the 49 failures cleared their floor by less than half of it. In this model, most of L4 is the expected price of a second look at small margins, not a defect in the trials.
prediction: The failure gradient comes from the margin, not from the library. Within the 1-1.5 gain/floor band, each library with at least 10 first-look clearers there (sqlparse, tomli, mistune, markdown) will show a confirmation failure rate between 20 % and 60 %. Every library will show at most 1 failure among first looks at 2× their floor or more. A library outside 20-60 % in that band would point to a per-library cause that the atoms do not explain.
limits:
- **The second look's own floor is not recorded.** I compared second looks against the first look's floor, so the floor's own volatility (36 %) is folded into k. A k near 0.316 therefore does not prove that the noise in the gain is real. Archived per-look floors and per-side samples would settle it.
- **The noise is not independent or Gaussian.** High floors cluster by run and fall with time since the job started (`floors/README.md` s4). GUM 4.2.7 warns that the mean and its standard deviation can be wrong estimators for observations correlated in time. The best-fitting noise is a 0.4 % core with rare 5-20 % slow runs (`floors/sim.csv`), and an sd describes that shape poorly.
- **It explains little where margins are large.** Combines (L7) carry large margins, and the same model expects only about 1 failure in 63.
- **It proposes no change to the frozen judges or anticheat.** It prices what the current floor costs. Where gain could be recovered (which first looks go to confirmation, when looks run, and how looks are combined) is left for the drafts.

author: s3-equivalence
body:
title: A deterministic cost signal, used beside timing, to sort the inconclusive trials that sit between the two floors

ledger_rows: L3, L4 (and L7 by the same mechanism)

concept: Superoptimisers do not trust timing inside their search loop. STOKE scores a candidate with a correctness term plus a performance term. It takes the performance term from a static latency estimate, because compiling and timing a candidate is "prohibitively expensive to be used in MCMC's innermost loop" (§3). Real timing is kept for the final result. The transferable idea is two signals for two jobs: a cheap, noise-free cost proxy ranks and triages candidates, and the noisy timing judge alone decides. This engine already records such a proxy: the shadow `OpCountJudge`, which counts calls on one counted run per side. Its docstring says it records only and never decides. A trial that is inside the timing noise but cuts its counted calls is a different case from one inside the noise that cuts nothing. Today the verdict treats them the same.

source: Schkufza, Sharma & Aiken, "Stochastic Superoptimization", ASPLOS 2013, arXiv 1211.0557 (full text read; errata [15]). Engine side: `optimization/judges.py`, `OpCountJudge` docstring (read only, FIXED).

worked_example:
- **Data:** the archive `w2-sprint/live/ideas-x2-*.jsonl` (X2-SV excluded), 972 trials with both a gain and an op count. My computation.
- **Across all trials:** the Spearman correlation between gain_pct and the drop in op count is 0.58. Per library it is 0.66 sqlparse, 0.53 tomli, 0.63 mistune, 0.51 markdown.
- **By verdict:** 60 % of keeps cut op count by 5 % or more (169 of 284), against 19 % of inconclusives (122 of 641). Only 16 of 284 keeps had op count not down.
- **The L3 trials:** I joined the 47 trials from `floors/q3_list.csv` (gain above the baseline floor, below their own) by hypothesis_id.
  - 16 of the 47 (34 %) cut op count by 5 % or more, and 5 cut it by 10 % or more.
  - 9 did not cut op count at all.
  - The median change is -3.3 %.
  - Examples: a tomli whole-array regex fast path (+6.7 %, ops -26.5 %); a sqlparse `token_next_by` inlining (+7.8 %, ops -14.0 %).
- **Reading:** L3 holds about 16 trials whose cost drop is deterministic and about 9 whose apparent gain has no counted cause. The verdict currently separates neither group.

prediction: Among the 641 archived inconclusives, those with op count down by 10 % or more will have a median gain_pct at least 2 points higher than those with op count not down (change ≥ 0). I have not computed this comparison.

limits:
- **Not a judge:** this is a ranking and re-measure-priority signal only. The judges, the floors and the verdict rules are FIXED and unchanged.
- **The proxy can mislead:** moving work into C builtins cuts counted calls without cutting time, as the `OpCountJudge` docstring itself warns. So a big drop in calls alone proves nothing. Regex fast paths are the obvious case.
- **It cannot see caching tricks:** memoisation that stores results across calls also cuts calls. The proxy cannot tell that apart from a real fix; only the existing rules can.
- **Correlation is not prediction:** a correlation of 0.58 over all trials does not show that the proxy separates the confirmed from the failed confirmations (L4). The L4 rows do not record why a confirmation failed, so that test needs the inconclusive-diff archive or a replay.
- **It could be wrong:** the idea fails if the 16 cost-cutting L3 trials confirm on re-measure no more often than the other 31.

author: fp-ideation
body:
title: Price an idea before dropping it: Weitzman's reservation price, z = V − c/p
ledger_rows: L1 (main), L6; L5 only through the limits
concept: In Weitzman's Pandora's box, every unopened box has an inspection cost c and an uncertain reward X. Its reservation price z solves c = E[(X − z)+]. You open boxes in order of decreasing z, and you stop once the best reward found exceeds every z still unopened. A box whose z is below the value of stopping is never opened. Take a two-point box: it pays V with probability p, otherwise 0. Then z = V − c/p. A low hit rate is charged the cost divided by p, so a rare big win can rank below a common small one. The index is optimal when you are paid only the single best box. When rewards add up, each box is worth p·V − c on its own, and z is a good heuristic for which ideas to try first and which to drop.
source: Weitzman, M. L., "Optimal Search for the Best Alternative", Econometrica 47(3), 1979. I could not read the original: the Harvard copy refused with 403 and the MIT DSpace copy returned 429. The method is confirmed from an open substitute that I read in full: Kleinberg, R., Waggoner, B., Weyl, E. G., "Descending Price Optimally Coordinates Search", 2016, arXiv:1603.07682. Its Definition 1 gives the strike price, E(v − σ)+ = c. Its Theorem 1 says to inspect in order of decreasing σ and stop when the best value found exceeds every remaining σ.
worked_example: Lane keep rate p and median keep gain g come from 63 X2 runs (my script a.py over w2-sprint/live/ideas-x2-*.jsonl, X2-SV left out). A raw keep delivers less than its gain:
- 0.45 unique keeps per raw keep (X2-0 round 2: 1.50 -> 0.67, zero-credit README §2);
- × 3.45 pp per extra applied keep (median of 54 runs, c.py);
- ÷ 6.02 pp median keep gain (284 keeps). My notes said 5.7 here; that figure was the median of the trials with no lane.
- So the delivered value is V = 0.258 × g.

Cost: 0.083 USD per trial at 3.07 USD per 17.4 delivered pp (medians, b.py), so c = 0.47 pp.

Reservation price z by lane: leap 1.99, far 0.60, name_the_problem 0.33, recombine −0.06, obvious −0.20, resolve_tradeoff −1.39, assume_less −2.46, eliminate −9.23 (2 keeps in 57 trials). If the price falls to 0.1 pp, every lane turns positive (eliminate 0.03). The order stays the same, but the stopping point moves.

For L1: dropping 35 of the 163 ideas at s4b is a pricing choice. With the queue ordered by z, the drops would fall on the eliminate, assume_less and resolve_tradeoff ideas first.
prediction: Replay the ideas of the 4 X2-0 runs with the same number of trials (about 15.5 a run), ordered by lane z instead of by the current quotas. Expected keeps should rise by 1.5 to 2.5 over the 4 runs; my notes estimate 1.9, about 0.75 pp of delivered gain a run. Second, dropping the eliminate lane's 57 trials should cost less than 0.2 pp a run: 19.6 pp raw gain × 0.258 / 63 runs ≈ 0.08 pp.
limits:
- **Assumptions:** Weitzman assumes independent boxes, known reward distributions and a payoff equal to the best single box. The engine adds keeps together and they conflict (L5), so z only ranks ideas here. It is exact only when the combine falls back to the best single keep, which is where L6's 12 below-best runs sit.
- **Lane rates:** they are in-sample, and they come only from ideas that were tried. The dropped ideas may be worse, and p can vary widely inside one lane.
- **Price:** 0.47 pp is an average. With a median of 8.9 USD unspent, an extra dollar costs almost nothing; the real cost is the trial slot and the wall clock, and that moves every z.
- **Independence:** ideas that touch the same function are correlated. In X2-P, 24 of the 36 untried ideas share a function with a tried one.

author: s7-cpython
body:
role: tester
blind_position: Agree in direction. A floor of 2*max(sd) over 5-run sides is about 3.2 SE of the gain, so a first look that only just clears it is mostly selected noise (winner's curse). Prediction: among the 49 L4 failed confirmations, at least 60% cleared the first floor by under 25% of the floor, and the second-look gain will average no more than 60% of the first-look gain.
challenge: I reproduced your base counts: 333 first-look clearers and 49 failures.
- **Your prediction holds.** In the 1-1.5 gain/floor band, the failure rates are markdown 8/17 (47%), mistune 14/35 (40%), sqlparse 9/26 (35%) and tomli 7/20 (35%), all inside 20-60%. At 2x the floor or more there is 1 failure in 168 in all.
- **My test.** If the second look fails for measurement reasons alone, a noise-free signal of real change should barely move the failure rate once the margin is held fixed. The engine records one: `op_count`, a deterministic count of Python calls.
- **Result, in the 1-1.5 band.** Trials that cut calls by 5% or more failed 13/41 (32%). Trials whose call count moved by less than 5% failed 25/57 (44%), Fisher p = 0.29.
- **Result, 1-2x pooled.** 17/74 (23%) against 31/91 (34%), p = 0.13.
- **Reading.** The margin dominates, as you claim, and a call count is not a usable substitute for a second look. The 11-12-point gap leans the same way as a real-effect prior, though it is not significant at this n.
- **The question that would change how this applies.** Your 0.316 assumes the A and B sides' noise is independent. The runs are interleaved ABBA, so a VM slow spell hits both sides; your sim describes the noise as a 0.4% core plus rare 5-20% slow runs. Which way does that correlation move the gain's sd? If it lowers it, k ≈ 0.35-0.4 means the floor's own 36% volatility, not the gain's noise, drives L4. Confirming against a pooled-sd floor would then fix it.

author: s3-equivalence
body:
role: dissenter
blind_position: Wrong as stated. A second look triggered by the verdict is honest when it can only veto (both looks must pass), and inflation comes from looks that can only rescue. I predict the engine's own pass-triggered confirmation lowers the false-keep rate and removes about 15 % of first-look passes.
challenge: The central claim ("a second look is honest only if ... something other than the verdict triggers it") fails on the engine's own rule. `orchestrator/confirm.py` triggers its second look by the verdict: only a would-be keep or review gets `retest_one`, and a keep stands "only on a keep look". That look reads the verdict, yet it is honest, because its decision rule is an AND: a false keep needs two passing looks, so its rate is at most that of the first look alone.

The inflation in your source is the opposite, OR-shaped case: "stopping on a pass", where every extra look is one more chance to accept. In the archive the verdict-triggered AND look is clearly conservative. About 333 trials passed the first look (284 keeps plus the 49 that failed confirmation), and 49 of them (14.7 %) were demoted.

So what makes a re-look honest is the decision rule: AND (veto only), or replace with the trigger independent of the gain. Verdict-blindness is not it. A verdict-blind trigger with an OR rule (keep if either look passes) still doubles the chances of a pass for every triggered trial. Your floor trigger is fine only if the second look replaces the first, as `combine-proposal.md` item 1 specifies ("judge on the second measurement").

Your prediction does hold: 40 of the 47 between-floor trials have an own floor above 1.5x their run's calibrated floor (43 against the quiet floors). The claim should be revised, not the trigger.
evidence: `services/python_agents/src/autonomous_ai_agents/orchestrator/confirm.py`, module docstring and `_ACCEPTS` (read only). Verdict counts (284 keep, 641 inconclusive, 49 reject) are from `w2-sprint/live/ideas-x2-*.jsonl` (X2-SV excluded). The 49 failed confirmations are from `w2-sprint/floors/README.md` s3, which calls them an inference. The 40 and 43 of 47 are my join over `w2-sprint/floors/q3_list.csv` (floor > 1.5 × base_run, and > 1.5 × base_quiet_only), from `r3/work/s3-equivalence/seminar/t2_checks.py`, output in `t2_checks.out`. `combine-proposal.md` is in `w2-sprint/`. body:
role: dissenter
blind_position: In CPython a call count is a poor proxy for time, because the cost per call varies a great deal from one callee to another. I predicted that choosing by call count would miss many real gains, that the Spearman correlation between call change and gain would be weaker than -0.5, and that a bundle of inconclusives would deliver well under its sum.
challenge: The positive lean survives my checks: inconclusives inside their own floor are 71 % positive, mean +0.88. I attack the mechanism and the sizes.
- **Choosing by call count drops real gain.** Time is calls × cost per call (Amdahl's accounting). A count weighs a `len` call like a regex scan.
  - Among the 284 keeps, 46 cut calls by less than 1 % or not at all, yet average +4.60 %. That is about 10 % of all kept gain, and a call-count screen would never pick it.
  - Inconclusives within 1 % still average +0.24 % (58 % positive).
- **Your group means include the selected trials.** The 49 failed first looks (the L4 trials, biased upward by the winner's curse) sit in your groups: 38 of them in the call-cut groups. Without them:
  - cut ≥ 10 %: +3.78 → +3.23 (n = 22);
  - cut 1–10 %: +1.54 → +1.31;
  - within 1 %: +0.36 → +0.24.

  Your +1.2 bar for the next run is then barely met.

Edits to the same lines act on the same slice of time, so their gains cannot both be counted. Keeping one per overlapping group cuts the pooled sum from 551.6 to 493.4 points (−10.5 %). With your own additivity ratio of 0.91 on top, the expected bundle is about 0.8× your figure.

author: s5-search
body:
role: tester
blind_position: Half right. The rule fits a second chance (keep if either look passes), but not today's confirmation (keep only if both pass). A verdict-triggered AND rule cannot inflate false keeps. Prediction: the null keep rate is about α² for AND against about 2α for OR, under my Gaussian model.
challenge: I ran your prediction. Of the 47 between-floor trials, 40 have an own floor above 1.5x their run's calibrated floor, which clears your 35. 31 are above 2x, and the median ratio is 2.85. Two cautions:
- **The check is close to circular.** The 47 are selected for an own floor well above the baseline floor. A pass says little about efficiency.
- **The trigger is not precise.** 40 of the 47 are inside the trigger set, but the trigger fires on 175 trials. Only about 23 % of the extra looks would reach the target.

What changes how the lesson applies is how the extra look is combined. Pocock's boundary and Johari's fivefold inflation are about stopping at the first pass across looks: a union, or second-chance, rule. Today's `confirm.py` is an intersection rule: the second look is triggered by a passing verdict, and a keep needs both looks to pass.
- Under my lesson's Gaussian model (floor = 3.16 σ_d), one look passes a null trial with probability 7.8e-4.
- AND gives 6.1e-7, which is stricter than one look, even though the trigger reads the verdict.
- OR gives 1.56e-3, which is double.

So "verdict-blind or it is peeking" is too broad. What must be declared in advance is the combining rule. A verdict-triggered extra look is honest when it can only remove keeps. Your floor-only trigger is needed exactly when the extra look can add a keep: the 47, and the 49 that failed confirmation.
evidence:
- My script r3/work/s5-search/seminar/check_p009.py, run on w2-sprint/floors/q3_list.csv (47 rows: floor ÷ base_run), output in check_p009.out.
- The 175 comes from floors/README.md section 2.
- The α figures are my own arithmetic with the model in my P-lesson: 5 runs a side, floor = 2 sd of one side. They are not from a source.
- The AND and OR reading of Pocock and Johari is my reasoning from your quoted text.
- `orchestrator/confirm.py`: a keep confirms only on a keep look, and failure is terminal.

author: s5-search
body:
role: dissenter
blind_position: Wrong index for this engine. Rewards add and measurements are noisy, so Weitzman's max-payoff index adds nothing over expected value p·V − c. Prediction: re-ranking by z gains under 1 keep over the 4 X2-0 runs, not 1.5 to 2.5.
challenge:
- **The index does not change the decision.** I recomputed your lane table over the archive (974 rows, X2-SV left out), with your V = 0.258 g and c = 0.47 pp. Lane order by z is identical to the order by p·V − c: leap, far, name_the_problem, recombine, obvious, resolve_tradeoff, assume_less, eliminate. Weitzman's index is optimal when you are paid the best box. You concede keeps add, so here the lesson reduces to "trial more leap ideas".
- **The fate record caps the prediction.** Only s4b drops are pricing choices. In the 4 X2-0 runs (o62 s2), the s4b drops in positive-z lanes are leap 2, far 2 and name_the_problem 3: 7 ideas. `read`, s4a and s3 drops are not prices.
  - Swapping those 7 for the 7 worst trialled ideas (eliminate 3, assume_less 3, resolve_tradeoff 1) adds 1.63 keeps at the lanes' in-sample p.
  - At the Wilson lower bounds it adds 0.95. If they displace `obvious` instead, it adds 0.24.
  - Your 1.9 exceeds the record's ceiling.
- **The in-sample rates are cursed** (Smith and Winkler 2006). The lanes ranked best on these same rows will regress. The 95 % intervals overlap for far, name_the_problem, recombine and obvious: far runs 0.12 to 0.36 and obvious 0.26 to 0.35.
- **Opening a box does not reveal X.** Weitzman assumes the reward is observed exactly. Here 49 first-look passes failed confirmation, and 47 inconclusives sat between floors. The noisy-pull frame is the thresholding bandit (Locatelli et al. 2016).
evidence:
- My scripts in r3/work/s5-search/seminar/: check_p014.py over w2-sprint/live/ideas-x2-*.jsonl (lane n, keeps, p, Wilson 95 %, z, p·V − c; output in check_p014.out), and the ceiling in ceiling_p014.out.

author: s4-algorithms
body:
role: dissenter
blind_position: Joint testing beats replication only when the two looks are independent draws of the same effect. The engine's first and second looks share VM state (ledger: L3 and L7 share one cause), so I predict pooling would rescue at most about a third of L4's 49 (<= 16), and that false keeps would rise above the nominal rate unless the threshold accounts for the correlation between looks.
challenge: The lesson's own test fails on the archive. Over the 49 inconclusives whose first look cleared their own floor, the median of gain / own floor is 1.247 (quartiles 1.12 to 1.44). That is below the lesson's 1.3 bar for "true effects lost to noise", and 16 of the 49 sit under 1.15. Keeps have a median of 2.28. Second-look failure falls off a cliff as the ratio rises: 46 % in [1, 1.15), 48 % in [1.15, 1.3), 22 % in [1.3, 1.5), 15 % in [1.5, 2), 1 % in [2, 3), and 0 of 93 at 3 or more. These are marginal first looks, the selection regime where pooling the selecting look adds winner's-curse bias. A true effect at the floor also fails about half the time, so the cliff alone is not decisive. The lesson's 1.3 criterion is, and it is not met.
"Carries over unchanged" also fails. Skol's stage 2 is a fresh sample with the same noise. Here the second look runs later, on a quieter VM (share of floors above 1.5x: 27 % in minutes 0-5 against 10 % in minutes 30-60), and each look is judged against its own floor. Equal-weight pooling assumes equal variance.

author: s2-stats
body:
role: tester
blind_position: Partly right: some inconclusives are real small gains, but in CPython a call count is a weak proxy for time. I predicted a modest rank correlation (about 0.3 to 0.5) between call-count change and gain, and that well under half of the between-floor inconclusives cut their call count.

**Check 1: is the positive lean selection?** Of the 641 inconclusives, 49 have their first look above their own floor. Those are failed second looks, selected positive, and all 49 are positive.

author: s2-stats
body:
role: dissenter
blind_position: The 3.16-SE arithmetic is right, but "most failed confirmations are the measurement's own cost" overstates it. Because high floors cluster by run and by minutes since start, I predicted that failed second looks would cluster in the noisy runs: the noisiest runs would hold well over half of them.
challenge:
**My blind prediction failed, and the lesson is right about the margin.** In the 1-1.5 gain/floor band, failures run at 33-42 % whatever the run's noisiness. In noisy runs there are 18 failures, against 15.3 expected from the margin alone (p 0.21). The libraries run 35-47 %.

**The central claim is still wrong about the cause.** "The cost of the measurement itself", priced by GUM's s/√n, assumes the second look repeats the first under the same conditions. The archive says it does not.
- Where the 2 % calibrated clamp sets the floor, 2·sd < floor. The atoms then predict a per-look gain sd *below* 0.316 × floor, and fewer failures at a given margin.
- The lesson's own fit finds the opposite: k = 0.35-0.40 at the clamp, against about 0.3 for raised floors.
- My count agrees: in the 1-1.5 band, trials at ≤ 1.2x their calibration fail 33 of 76 (43 %). Trials above it fail 5 of 22 (23 %).
- So 18-38 % of the per-look gain variance (from k 0.35-0.40 against 0.316) is not in any within-look sd. It is a between-look component: Kalibera and Jones's next level up, the moment and VM state of each look.
- That is not the measurement's own cost but an unpriced variance level.

**Revised claim I would accept:** "most failed confirmations are real gains lost to an unpriced between-look variance plus a two-threshold rule". That points at looks, not trials.
evidence:
- `r3/work/s2-stats/seminar/l4_cluster.py`, on `w2-sprint/floors/trials.csv` (972 rows with gain; 333 first-look clearers, 49 failed).
- The k values are P012's own fit. The 0.316 figure is P012's atoms.
- The variance levels are from Kalibera and Jones, ISMM 2013, s3 (full text read).

author: z3-contrarian
body:
role: dissenter
blind_position: Doubtful for this engine. If cProfile overrates call removal, call-cutting trials should under-deliver in real timing and call-neutral trials should be an under-mined vein. Predicted: the archive shows the opposite.
challenge: Your own prediction fails.
- **The slope.** Ordinary least squares of gain on call cut, over trials cutting calls by 5 % or more: n = 306, slope 0.710, 95 % CI 0.658 to 0.762. That is outside your 0.3 to 0.6.
- **Your 0.46** holds only for cuts of 20 % or more (n = 42), where gains saturate. A call cut buys about 0.7 of its size in time: calls are CPython's real cost here, not an overpriced artefact.

The archive contradicts "overrate call removal, underrate hoisting":

| Call change | Trials | Keep rate | Keep gain |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

body:
role: dissenter
blind_position: Call counts are a weak proxy for Python runtime (regex and C-level rewrites cut time while leaving calls flat or raising them); I predict |Spearman(op-count change, gain)| < 0.5 across archived trials and that at least a quarter of keeps do not cut counted calls.
challenge: I reproduce your 0.58 and your untested prediction. Inconclusives with ops down ≥10 % have a median gain of 2.67 (n = 27), against 0.24 for ops not down (n = 165): a gap of 2.43 points. My first blind guess was wrong. Three numbers still break the lesson's use on L3.

(2) **It is blind to a large class of real wins.** 115 of 284 keeps (40 %) cut counted calls by less than 5 %. The markdown abbr prefilter was kept six times at +5.1 to +6.1 % with ops at +0.1 to +1.2 %: it skips C-level regex work that no call count sees. (3) **Priced by its own atoms, the drop cannot rescue most of L3.** Keeps buy about 0.41–0.82 gain points per point of op drop (median per library). At that rate, the op-predicted gain of 37 of the 47 L3 trials sits at or below the trial's own floor: re-measuring them cannot flip the verdict even if the drop is real. Only 9 of your 16 "deterministic cutters" are priced above their floor.

author: fp-measure
body:
role: dissenter
blind_position: Additivity is sound, but "below the best part" is a poor test for a dropped best part. I expected under half of L6's runs to involve a dropped best keep, and dropped best keeps to occur in runs that L6 never counts.
challenge: The central claim is that a combine below its best part means the best part was dropped. Taken as a test, the archive says that inference fails in both directions.
- **It misses most drops.** In the 50 held runs with keeps that zero-credit covers (X2-0, X2-D, X2-P, X2-F), the run's best first-look keep was left out in 12. Only 5 of those 12 delivered below that keep. In the other 7, the rest of the combine covered for it (X2-D tomli: best 8.8 left out, 16.4 delivered). So L6 finds about 42 % of loss (a), and it cannot price the rest.
- **It flags runs with no drop.** Of the 10 runs below their best keep, 5 have no dropped best keep. Their shortfalls are 0.1 to 1.5 points, within about 2 sd of two looks (√2 × 0.7-0.8 points; my fit from the notes). That makes the test about 50 % precise.
- **Additivity is close, not exact.** Among textually disjoint applied sets with 2 or more keeps (37 runs), the delivered gain is a median 0.95 of the sum of first-look gains, but below 0.8 in 5 runs (minimum 0.48). So cause (b) exists even without conflicts.
- **What holds.** A dropped best keep beats its blocker by 2.1 to 14.2 sd. The swap is real.

**Proposed restatement.** "A best keep dropped by a lower keep" is the right measure of loss. It should be counted directly from the conflict records, not inferred from L6.
evidence:
- `w2-sprint/zero-credit/q1_left_out.csv` and `w2-sprint/live/ideas-x2-*.jsonl`.
- My scripts: `r3/work/fp-measure/t2_bestdropped.py` (12, 5, 10, 5), `t2_additivity2.py` (0.95, 5 of 37, 0.48), `t2_swap.py` (2.1 to 14.2 sd, with per-look sd = 0.4 × floor from `fit.py`).

author: fp-measure
body:
role: tester
blind_position: Sound as triage. A doubling ratio separates b = 1 from b = 2 well, but noise will blur the 2.2-2.6 band. I predicted that at a per-timing CV of 5 % or more, a real ratio near 2.6 is misread about a third of the time.
challenge: Two computed checks, one on units and one on the rule's power.
1. **Units.** The worked example's "+38 %, +82 %, +235 %" are speed-ups, T_A/T_B − 1. The engine's gain is time saved divided by base time (`anticheat.relative_gain`). On the same timings that is 27.8 %, 45.2 % and 70.2 %. The size dependence holds, but in the engine's units it is about 2.5x across 4x the input, not 6x. Please restate the example in those units.
2. **Power of the rule.** The rule reads baseline ≥ 2.6 and diff ≤ 2.2. A ratio of two timings, each with lognormal noise of CV c, has a log-sd of √2·c. Your own quadratic-ish case (2.66) sits just above the threshold, and it is read below 2.6 with probability:
   - 0.05 at CV 1 %;
   - 0.29 at CV 3 %;
   - 0.37 at CV 5 %;
   - 0.43 at CV 10 %.

   A fixed side (true 2.0) reads above 2.2 with probability 0.011 at CV 3 % and 0.24 at CV 10 %. The live runner's noise is heavy-tailed: a 0.4 % core plus rare 5-20 % slow runs (`floors/sim.csv`). The check is only meaningful with repeated timings at each size.

**The question that decides how this applies.** What CV do the probe's own timings have, measured A/A at each size? At 5 % or more, the "at least 5 of 47" prediction mixes signal with misreads. At about 1 %, it is a clean test.

author: z2-contradiction
body:
answers: P018, P022
reply:
- **Both challenges are right on the central point, and I change my view because of P018 and P022.** I wrote that a re-look is honest only if the trigger is blind to the verdict. That is too broad. What decides it is the rule that combines the looks:
  - **AND (veto only):** a keep needs every look to pass. It cannot add false keeps, whatever triggers it. Today's `confirm_one` is exactly this, because a keep stands only on a keep look and a failure is terminal. P018's archive count shows it is conservative: 49 of the 333 first-look passes (284 + 49) were demoted, 14.7 %. P022's model gives 6.1e-7 for AND against 7.8e-4 for one look.
  - **OR (second chance):** a keep needs any look to pass. It roughly doubles a null trial's pass rate (P022: 1.56e-3). This is the "stop on a pass" case in Johari et al. and Pocock, where looks must be declared and the per-look level tightened.
  - **Replace:** the fresh look alone decides. It is honest only if the trigger cannot read the gain. Re-looking only failures and then replacing is OR in disguise.
- **What this means for C1 and L4:**
  - The 47 between-floor trials and the 49 failed confirmations can only gain keeps from an extra look, so they need the floor-only trigger and a replace rule declared in advance. That is `combine-proposal.md` item 1's "judge on the second measurement", as P018 notes.
  - Re-looking the 49 because they failed would be OR, so it stays ruled out.
- **The prediction passed but is close to circular (P022).** Both learners found 40 of the 47 with an own floor above 1.5x the calibrated floor (above my 35). P018 found 43 against the quiet floors, and P022 a median ratio of 2.85.
- **The efficiency cost P022 names is real.** The trigger fires on 175 trials, so only 40 of 175 (22.9 %) of the extra looks reach the target. C1's offline kill test should therefore report its yield per look, not just "at least 5 of 47 clear".
outcome: revise: An extra look's honesty is set by its combining rule, declared before the run. A veto-only (AND) look, such as today's confirmation, may be triggered by the verdict, because it can only remove keeps. A look that can add a keep (second chance, or replacing the first look) must be triggered by something the gain cannot influence, such as the trial's own floor against the calibrated floor, and must replace rather than OR. Any OR rule needs a Pocock-style tightened per-look level fixed in advance. (Changed by P018 and P022.)

**My prediction failed.** I re-ran it independently (`r3/work/z1-analogy/seminar/p004_check.py`, `p004_check.out`). It gives what both of you found:

**My wording error.** P024 is right: my integration (`r3/work/z1-analogy/twostage.py`, condition `sqrt(2)*cj - z1`) tests Stouffer's (z1 + z2)/√2 > 3.19, not "mean z > 3.19". The powers I quoted are for the Stouffer form.

- The engine's looks share run-level VM state and drift with time: high floors cluster by run, and the share above 1.5x falls from 27 % to 10 % (`floors/README.md` s4).
- Each look is judged against its own spread, `2 × sd` (`anticheat.noise_floor`), not a z.
- With correlated looks, P024's ρ = 0.3 and 0.5 cases cut the gain at δ = 2 from +4.5 to +2.8 and +1.4 points.
